# Introduction

In this homework I import data into R from different sources: CSV and text
files, Excel, statistical packages (SPSS, Stata, SAS), a MySQL database,
a web API, and a few other sources like XML and a web page.

First I create a small data frame of students and save it in the different
file formats. Then I import each file back into R, one format at a time.
The database part reads from a MySQL database called `simba`.

```{r packages}
# Every package used in this document. Installing them here means the file
# also knits on a computer that does not have them yet.
pkgs <- c("readr", "readxl", "writexl", "haven", "DBI",
          "RMariaDB", "jsonlite", "xml2", "rvest")

# installed.packages() lists what is already on this machine, so this keeps
# only the names that are missing and installs those.
new_pkgs <- pkgs[!pkgs %in% rownames(installed.packages())]
if (length(new_pkgs) > 0) install.packages(new_pkgs, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")

library(readr)     # read_csv(), faster CSV reading
library(readxl)    # read_excel()
library(writexl)   # write_xlsx()
library(haven)     # SPSS, Stata and SAS files
library(DBI)       # databases
library(jsonlite)  # JSON, used for the API
library(xml2)      # XML
library(rvest)     # web scraping
```

# Creating the data

Everything starts from one small table of eight students. I build it with
`data.frame()`: each argument becomes one column, and `c()` holds the values
of that column.

```{r make-data}
students <- data.frame(
  id      = 1:8,
  name    = c("Aline", "Eric", "Grace", "Jean", "Kevin", "Diane", "Olivier", "Sandra"),
  gender  = c("F", "M", "F", "M", "M", "F", "M", "F"),
  age     = c(23, 27, 25, 31, 24, 29, 26, 28),
  program = c("MSc IT", "MSc DS", "MSc DS", "MBA", "MSc IT", "MSc DS", "MBA", "MSc IT"),
  score   = c(78.5, 85.0, 91.5, 66.0, 72.5, 88.0, 59.5, 81.0)
)
students
```

Now I save that same table in six different formats. This gives me real files
to import in the rest of the homework, instead of looking for files somewhere
on the computer.

```{r save-files}
# showWarnings = FALSE stops R from complaining when the folder already exists
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

# row.names = FALSE keeps R from adding an extra column of row numbers
write.csv(students, "data/students.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# sep = "\t" writes a tab between the columns instead of a comma
write.table(students, "data/students.txt", sep = "\t", row.names = FALSE)

write_xlsx(students, "data/students.xlsx")   # Excel

write_sav(students, "data/students.sav")     # SPSS
write_dta(students, "data/students.dta")     # Stata
write_xpt(students, "data/students.xpt")     # SAS transport file

list.files("data")
```

Note that all the paths are written as `data/students.csv` and not as a full
path like `/Users/me/Documents/...`. A short path like that is relative to the
folder holding this file, so the document still works when somebody else opens
the project on their own computer.

# CSV and text files

A CSV is just a text file where a comma separates the columns. `read.csv()`
is the base R function for it, and it gives back a normal data frame.

```{r csv}
csv_data <- read.csv("data/students.csv")

# str() is the quickest way to check an import went well: it shows how many
# rows and columns arrived, and the type R gave to each column.
str(csv_data)
```

The `readr` package does the same job but is faster on big files and returns a
tibble, which is a data frame that prints more neatly and shows column types.

```{r csv-readr}
csv_data2 <- read_csv("data/students.csv")
csv_data2
```

The text file uses tabs instead of commas, so I have to say so. `header = TRUE`
tells R that the first line holds the column names and is not data.

```{r txt}
txt_data <- read.table("data/students.txt", header = TRUE, sep = "\t")
head(txt_data)
```

# Excel files

An Excel file can hold several sheets, so the first thing to do is look at what
is inside before reading anything.

```{r excel}
excel_sheets("data/students.xlsx")

# With only one sheet I can leave the sheet argument out. For a file with
# several sheets I would write sheet = "students" or sheet = 2.
excel_data <- read_excel("data/students.xlsx")
head(excel_data)
```

# Statistical packages (SPSS, Stata, SAS)

`haven` reads files from all three programs. The function changes with the
program: `read_sav()` for SPSS, `read_dta()` for Stata, and `read_xpt()` or
`read_sas()` for SAS.

## SPSS

```{r spss}
spss_data <- read_sav("data/students.sav")
head(spss_data)
```

## Stata

```{r stata}
stata_data <- read_dta("data/students.dta")
head(stata_data)
```

## SAS

```{r sas}
sas_data <- read_xpt("data/students.xpt")
head(sas_data)
```

A real SAS data file ends in `.sas7bdat` and needs `read_sas()`. I do not have
one, but `haven` ships with an example, and `system.file()` finds where that
example was installed.

```{r sas7bdat}
sas_iris <- read_sas(system.file("examples", "iris.sas7bdat", package = "haven"))
head(sas_iris)
```

## Labelled values

One thing is different about files from these programs, and it catches people
out. SPSS and Stata usually store a category as a *number with a label
attached*: the file holds 1 and 2, and remembers separately that 1 means
Female and 2 means Male. My own file above was written from plain text, so it
has no labels, but the SPSS example that comes with `haven` does.

```{r spss-labels}
iris_spss <- read_sav(system.file("examples", "iris.sav", package = "haven"))

# Species arrives as numbers 1, 2, 3 ...
head(iris_spss$Species)

# ... and the meaning of those numbers is kept as an attribute
attr(iris_spss$Species, "labels")
```

Counting those numbers directly would give a meaningless table, so
`as_factor()` swaps each number for its label and gives an ordinary R factor:

```{r spss-as-factor}
iris_spss$Species <- as_factor(iris_spss$Species)
table(iris_spss$Species)
```

# Database management system (MySQL)

R talks to databases through the `DBI` package plus a driver for the specific
database. For MySQL the driver is `RMariaDB`.

The database here is `simba`, running on my own machine. Since this homework
is in a public repository, I do not write the password in the code. R reads it
from environment variables instead, and falls back to the values I use locally
when those variables are not set. To set your own, put a line like
`SIMBA_PASSWORD=yourpassword` in a file called `.Renviron` in this folder and
restart R.

```{r mysql-connect}
db_host <- Sys.getenv("SIMBA_HOST", "127.0.0.1")
db_user <- Sys.getenv("SIMBA_USER", "root")
db_pass <- Sys.getenv("SIMBA_PASSWORD", "")
db_name <- Sys.getenv("SIMBA_DB",   "simba")

# try() means a failed connection does not stop the whole document. Anyone
# without this database still gets a knitted file; the database sections are
# simply skipped. See sql/01_create_simba_sample.sql to create the database.
con <- try(
  dbConnect(RMariaDB::MariaDB(),
            host = db_host, port = 3306,
            user = db_user, password = db_pass,
            dbname = db_name),
  silent = TRUE
)

# TRUE when the connection worked. The chunks below use it as eval = db_ok,
# which is how an R Markdown chunk is switched on or off.
db_ok <- !inherits(con, "try-error")
db_ok
```

```{r mysql-tables, eval=db_ok}
# What tables are in this database?
dbListTables(con)
```

The simplest way to import is to pull a whole table into R:

```{r mysql-table, eval=db_ok}
products <- dbReadTable(con, "products")
dim(products)   # rows, columns

head(products[, c("id", "name", "unit_price", "quantity_in_stock")])
```

Pulling the whole table is fine for a small one, but a real table can have
millions of rows. `dbGetQuery()` is the better habit: the database does the
filtering and only the answer travels back to R. Here I look for the products
that have run low and need to be ordered again.

```{r mysql-query, eval=db_ok}
low_stock <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT name, quantity_in_stock, reorder_level
  FROM products
  WHERE quantity_in_stock <= reorder_level
  ORDER BY quantity_in_stock")
low_stock
```

The same idea with a summary. Counting and averaging inside SQL is much faster
than bringing every row into R and doing it there.

```{r mysql-group, eval=db_ok}
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT category_id,
         COUNT(*)                     AS products,
         ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 0)    AS avg_price
  FROM products
  GROUP BY category_id")
```

When a value comes from outside, put a `?` in the query and pass the value
through `params`. The database then treats it as data and never as part of the
SQL, which is what stops SQL injection.

```{r mysql-param, eval=db_ok}
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT name, unit_price FROM products WHERE unit_price >= ?",
           params = list(2000))
```

```{r mysql-close, eval=db_ok}
# A connection is a real network socket, so close it when the work is done.
dbDisconnect(con)
```

Only the driver changes for another database system. Everything after
`dbConnect()` stays exactly the same:

| Database | Driver |
|----------|--------|
| MySQL / MariaDB | `RMariaDB::MariaDB()` |
| PostgreSQL | `RPostgres::Postgres()` |
| SQLite | `RSQLite::SQLite()` |
| SQL Server, Oracle, Access | `odbc::odbc()` |

# Web API

An API is a web address that returns data instead of a web page. The World
Bank has a free one, and this request asks for the total population of Rwanda
(country code `RW`). It answers in JSON, which `fromJSON()` turns into R
objects.

```{r api}
url <- "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/RW/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?format=json&per_page=30"
wb <- fromJSON(url)

# This API answers with a list of two parts: [[1]] is information about the
# page (how many results, which page) and [[2]] is the actual data.
rwanda_pop <- data.frame(year       = as.integer(wb[[2]]$date),
                         population = wb[[2]]$value)

# The API returns the newest year first, so I put it back in order
rwanda_pop <- rwanda_pop[order(rwanda_pop$year), ]
tail(rwanda_pop)
```

```{r api-plot}
# Dividing by 1e6 keeps the axis readable: millions instead of 14569341
plot(rwanda_pop$year, rwanda_pop$population / 1e6, type = "l",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Population (millions)",
     main = "Population of Rwanda")
```

# Other sources

## XML

XML stores data as a tree of tags. Instead of rows and columns you point at the
tags you want with a path, where `//name` means "every `<name>` tag anywhere in
the document".

```{r xml}
xml_string <- "<students>
  <student><name>Aline</name><score>78</score></student>
  <student><name>Eric</name><score>85</score></student>
  <student><name>Grace</name><score>91</score></student>
</students>"

doc <- read_xml(xml_string)

data.frame(
  name  = xml_text(xml_find_all(doc, "//name")),
  # everything arrives as text, so the scores need converting to numbers
  score = as.numeric(xml_text(xml_find_all(doc, "//score")))
)
```

## Web scraping

Sometimes the data is only on a web page. `rvest` downloads the page and pulls
the table out of the HTML.

```{r scraping}
page <- read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Rwanda")

# "table.wikitable" is the CSS selector for the first table with the
# wikitable class, which is the standard style for data tables on Wikipedia
provinces <- html_table(html_element(page, "table.wikitable"))
provinces[, 1:4]
```

## Built-in datasets

R also ships with datasets for practising. `data()` opens the full list in a
new tab in RStudio.

```{r builtin}
data(airquality)
head(airquality)
```

# Conclusion

Each source needs its own function: `read.csv()` for CSV, `read_excel()` for
Excel, `read_sav()` for SPSS, `dbGetQuery()` for a database, `fromJSON()` for
an API. What they all have in common is where they end: whatever the source,
the data lands in R as a data frame, which is the shape the rest of R expects
for cleaning, analysis and plotting.
